When Punctures Happen on Tour

A puncture on a remote Highland road with no mobile signal and no passing traffic is every tourer's nightmare. While tubeless tyres on modern touring bikes are less prone to catastrophic failure than tubed tyres, punctures still happen. Carrying a compact repair kit and knowing how to use it means the difference between a 20-minute roadside fix and a very expensive recovery callout.

Types of Repair

  • Plug kit (mushroom plugs) — The most common roadside repair. A reaming tool cleans the puncture hole, then a mushroom-shaped rubber plug is inserted from inside the tyre using an insertion tool. Quick, effective for nail-type punctures, and allows you to ride to a tyre fitter for a proper repair.
  • Rope plugs (string plugs) — Strips of sticky rubber inserted into the puncture using a needle tool. Quicker than mushroom plugs but generally considered less reliable for touring speeds. A temporary fix to get you to a garage.
  • Tyre sealant — Liquid sealant injected through the valve. Works for small punctures but can unbalance the tyre and makes proper repair more difficult. Best kept as an emergency backup.

Essential Kit Contents

A complete touring puncture repair kit should include:

Reaming tool for cleaning the puncture hole. Plug insertion tool for fitting mushroom or string plugs. Selection of plugs in various sizes. CO2 inflator with at least three cartridges (one cartridge typically adds about 20psi to a motorcycle tyre). Small tyre pressure gauge for checking inflation. Valve core removal tool for adding sealant if needed. Latex gloves to keep your hands clean.

Best Puncture Repair Kits

Stop and Go Pocket Tyre Plugger — Compact kit with mushroom plugs, CO2 inflator, and reaming tools. Fits easily in a pannier or tank bag. The mushroom plugs are among the most reliable available.

Dynaplug Racer Pro — Ultra-compact plug insertion tool that combines reaming and insertion in one step. Brass-tipped plugs insert cleanly and hold securely. Premium-priced but excellent quality.

Oxford CO2yre Repair Kit — Budget-friendly kit with string plugs and CO2 cartridges. Compact and effective for a temporary roadside repair.

Practice using your repair kit at home before you need it roadside. The first time you use a plug kit should not be in the rain on a remote Scottish B-road with fading daylight. Familiarity with the process makes roadside repairs quicker and less stressful.

After a Repair

A plug repair is a temporary fix. Ride cautiously to the nearest tyre fitter for a permanent internal repair or tyre replacement. Reduce your speed and avoid hard braking and acceleration. Check the plug every time you stop to ensure it is holding and the tyre pressure is stable. Read our Best Motorcycle Roads in Scotland: 15 Must-Ride Routes guide for more. Read our Cotswolds Motorcycle Touring Routes: Honey-Stone Villages and Rolling Hills guide for more.
keyTakeaways: Mushroom plug kits are the most reliable roadside repair for tubeless tyres.
Carry a CO2 inflator with at least three cartridges; one adds roughly 20psi to a bike tyre.
Rope plugs are quicker but less reliable at touring speeds; treat them as temporary.
Any plug repair is temporary; ride gently to a fitter for a permanent internal repair.
Practise using your kit at home before you ever need it on a remote roadside.

pros: A compact kit turns a 20-minute fix into an avoided recovery callout.
Mushroom plugs let you ride to a tyre fitter safely.
The whole kit fits easily in a pannier or tank bag.
cons: Plug repairs are temporary and need a proper follow-up repair.
Sealant can unbalance the tyre and complicate later repairs.
CO2 cartridges are single-use, so carry several spares.

faq.q: What should a touring puncture kit contain?
faq.a: A complete kit includes a reaming tool to clean the hole, a plug insertion tool, a selection of plugs in various sizes, a CO2 inflator with at least three cartridges, a small pressure gauge, a valve core removal tool and latex gloves. One CO2 cartridge typically adds around 20psi to a motorcycle tyre, so three lets you reach a usable pressure with margin to spare.

faq.q: Are mushroom plugs or rope plugs better?
faq.a: Mushroom plugs are more reliable for touring. A reaming tool cleans the hole, then the mushroom-shaped plug is inserted and seats securely, holding well at touring speeds. Rope or string plugs are quicker to fit but generally considered less reliable, so they are best treated as a temporary fix to reach a garage rather than a long-term repair.

faq.q: Is a plugged tyre safe to keep riding on?
faq.a: A plug is a temporary fix, not a permanent one. Ride cautiously to the nearest tyre fitter for a proper internal repair or replacement, reducing your speed and avoiding hard braking and acceleration. Check the plug and tyre pressure every time you stop to make sure it is holding. Do not treat a roadside plug as a permanent solution.

faq.q: Should I use tyre sealant instead of a plug?
faq.a: Sealant is best kept as an emergency backup rather than a primary repair. It works for small punctures but can unbalance the tyre and makes a proper repair harder later, as fitters have to clean it out. A plug kit is the more dependable roadside solution, with sealant carried only for punctures too awkward to plug.

faq.q: Why should I practise before I need it?
faq.a: The first time you use a plug kit should not be in the rain on a remote Scottish B-road with fading light. Reaming and inserting a plug takes a firm, confident technique that is much easier once you have done it before. Practise on an old tyre at home so that a real roadside puncture becomes a quick, calm job rather than a stressful ordeal.
